figures.name: John of Morigny
figures.name_full: John of Morigny (Latin: Johannes de Morigniaco)
figures.lifespan: fl. c. 1290s–1320s (no firm birth or death year established in the sources this portal has read)
figures.region: Abbey of Morigny, near Étampes; studied at Orléans
figures.card: A Benedictine monk and priest of the Abbey of Morigny, near Étampes, with an advanced degree in canon law from the University of Orléans. As a young monk he practiced the condemned ritual art called the *ars notoria* and dabbled in necromancy; a sequence of visions convinced him the practice was demonically contaminated, and he responded not by abandoning ritual magic but by **rewriting it** — composing the *Liber florum celestis doctrine* ("Flowers of Heavenly Teaching"), a purified prayer-and-vision system he claimed was authorized directly by the Virgin Mary. Condemned twice — by unnamed "Barking Dogs" in 1315, and at Paris in 1323, where the *Grandes Chroniques de France* records his book burned — his text nonetheless survived in over twenty manuscripts and circulated among monks for two centuries before vanishing from scholarship entirely until its rediscovery in the early 1990s.
figures.body:
John of Morigny was a fourteenth-century Benedictine monk attached to the Abbey of Morigny, near Étampes in northern France. He was a priest and a highly educated one: he held an advanced degree in canon law from the University of Orléans, and his surviving writing shows deep familiarity with the literature, liturgy, exegesis, and theology of the later Middle Ages (Fanger, *Rewriting Magic*, p.1). No firm birth or death year is established in the sources read for this portal; John is known almost entirely through the one book he left behind, and through the record of its condemnation.

Fanger's 2015 preface to *Rewriting Magic* corrects her own earlier published guess (a location at Chartres) about where John's *ars notoria* experiments took place: the evidence now points to **Orléans**, where he was sent to earn his canon-law degree, and where — as a professed monk — canon law and theology were the only two university subjects open to him (theology being reserved to Paris). Orléans put him within reach of the university book trade and, per Kieckhefer's phrase adopted across the field, its "clerical underworld" of student necromancy (*Rewriting Magic*, p.x–xi). Fanger and Watson also newly identify *Otrouiacum*, named in the Book of Visions as the location of John's mother's house, as Autruy-sur-Juine — a village on the Roman road between Morigny and Orléans, roughly midway between the two (*Rewriting Magic*, p.xi).

## The Ars Notoria Period and the Turn Away

John's own Book of Visions confesses to experimentation with both *nigromancia* (necromancy, or black magic) and the *ars notoria*, a widely used and widely condemned ritual system promising infused knowledge of the liberal arts, philosophy, and theology through prayer and the contemplation of geometric figures (*notae*) (*Rewriting Magic*, p.2). His conversion away from the practice was neither sudden nor total. After a vision (vision 8) in which God expressed unambiguous prohibition, John himself records that he "put it away from me somewhat, but not entirely" (*Rewriting Magic*, p.66, quoting the Book of Visions) — a moment Fanger reads as evidence the text is a genuine *confessio*, not a hagiographic conversion narrative smoothed of its false starts.

The vision that did finally and thoroughly turn him is vision 9, among the strangest episodes in the whole text. Troubled by disturbing visions and seeking to understand them, John recites a prayer from his old ars notoria book "which is said for memory, as the custom is." That night he dreams of driving off a malign spirit with a sword, then being approached by a tall man in ash-colored robes who asks *John* to hear his confession. The man confesses to having "dispensed mercy where I should have dispensed justice" and demands absolution; when John tries the ordinary words of absolution, the man refuses them — "open your mouth and I will fill it" — and John finds himself speaking words identifying the penitent as Christ himself (*Rex regum, princeps principum et dominus dominancium* — "king of kings, prince of princes, lord of lords"). John writes: "And then I understood, I knew without doubt, and I had proven by experience, that the book of the *ars notoria* was entirely malign" (*Rewriting Magic*, p.68–69, quoting Book of Visions). From this point, per his own account, he abandoned the *ars notoria* entirely, confessed, and began the work that became the *Liber florum*.

## Two Condemnations, and the Rewriting

The *Liber florum*'s composition was broken in the middle by two separate condemnations, eight years apart — a fact Fanger and Watson's own edition work uncovered and that earlier scholarship (built only on the famous 1323 burning) had missed entirely.

In **1315**, unnamed "Barking Dogs" — John's own term, apparently canon lawyers, never further identified — condemned his original Book of Figures, whose diagrams too closely resembled necromantic figures to their eyes. The book had already circulated to a community of operators; John could not simply recall it. Instead he composed a new installment: a rewritten Book of Figures offering an alternative ritual and spiritual process, leaning more heavily than before on direct visionary authorization from the Virgin (*Rewriting Magic*, p.2–3). This is the origin of the **New Compilation** — not a leisurely revision, but an urgent response to institutional attack, written, in Fanger's words, "in great haste." Internal evidence (successive strata visible in the prayers and the Book of Visions) shows the Old Compilation had itself already been revised at least once before 1315 (*Rewriting Magic*, p.118) — John was a compulsive reviser even before the condemnations forced his hand.

The second and more famous condemnation came in **1323**: an entry in the *Grandes Chroniques de France* records the burning at Paris of a book by an unnamed "monk of Morigny" who had sought to "inspire and renew a condemned heresy and sorcery called in Latin *ars notoria*" — a work described as securing all branches of knowledge, and "any riches, honours or pleasures one wanted to have," through figures contemplated with fasting and prayer and the invocation of "little known names" believed to be demons' names (*Rewriting Magic*, p.3). Fanger notes the description is in several ways unfair to the actual text — the *Liber florum* is explicitly not concerned with worldly riches or pleasures — but it does at least distinguish John's book from the *ars notoria* itself, a distinction later paraphrases would lose entirely (see [[historiography-of-erasure]]).

## Rewriting as Devotion, Not Retraction

What John does after each condemnation is the single most important fact about him as a historical actor: he does not stop. He does not recant the underlying claim that ritual access to divine knowledge is licit when properly authorized. He rewrites — producing a purified system explicitly modeled on the shape of the *ars notoria* he had practiced, but claiming its authorization directly from the Virgin Mary rather than from the older art's own textual tradition, and using a biblical trope from Augustine to justify plundering the old art's "sacred and divine words" for the new book, "as the Hebrews plundered the Egyptian treasure" (*Rewriting Magic*, p.2; see [[plundering-egyptian-treasure]]). The finished *Liber florum celestis doctrine* breaks into three parts — the Book of Visions (autobiography and apologia), the Book of Prayers (the ritual liturgy proper), and the Book of Figures (further visions and the diagrams themselves) — see [[liber-florum-celestis-doctrine]] for the full structure.

## Transmission and Survival

Contrary to the intuitive assumption that a public burning ends a text's life, the *Liber florum* did not stop circulating in 1323. Fanger argues that evidence of its continued transmission and ritual use among literate monks after 1323 — likely spread in part through Benedictine travel between houses — "challenges the widespread belief that book condemnation constitutes effective censorship" (*Rewriting Magic*, p.21–22; see [[censorship-does-not-work]]). As of Fanger's 2015 count, twenty-three manuscripts contain all or part of John's work: one preserves the Old Compilation, eighteen contain all or substantial portions of the New Compilation, and four are prayer-collections drawing unattributed sequences from it (*Rewriting Magic*, p.xi).

## Rediscovery

The *Liber florum* then effectively vanished from scholarship for over six centuries, known only through steadily degrading paraphrases of the 1323 chronicle notice (see [[historiography-of-erasure]]), until a convergence of independent rediscoveries in the early 1990s: Sylvie Barnay in France, and Nicholas Watson together with Claire Fanger in Canada, each independently located manuscripts containing the full New Compilation text (*Rewriting Magic*, p.21). Watson and Fanger's subsequent collaboration produced the first English-language scholarship on the text and, in 2015, the critical Latin edition (Fanger & Watson, *Liber florum celestis doctrine*, PIMS) that underlies most of what is now known about John.

figures.name: Bridget (Burgeta)
figures.name_full: Burgeta, called Bridget in earlier English-language scholarship
figures.lifespan: contemporary of John of Morigny, fl. early 14th c.
figures.card: John of Morigny's sister. The authoritative manuscript reading of her name is **Burgeta**, not "Gurgeta" or "Georgette" as she appeared in Fanger and Watson's own 2001 edition of the *Liber visionum* — a correction Fanger's 2015 preface explicitly issues (*Rewriting Magic*, p.x). She is one of two named witnesses — alongside John of Fontainejean — whose testimony against the *ars notoria* John records in the Book of Visions (I.iii). Her exact relationship to the practice itself (student, independent practitioner, or witness only) is not resolved in the sources read for this portal.
figures.body:
Bridget — whose name in the manuscript tradition Fanger and Watson now read as **Burgeta**, correcting their own earlier "Gurgeta" (itself sometimes anglicized "Georgette") from the 2001 edition of the *Liber visionum* — was John of Morigny's sister. She lived in the same Orléans–Étampes corridor John himself moved through as a student and later as a monk visiting his family; Fanger's 2015 preface notes John's location at Orléans "makes better sense... of the fact that he is evidently rubbing shoulders with friars and Cistercians (as well as visiting his sister)" during his university years and later during the composition of the Book of Prayers (*Rewriting Magic*, p.xi).

Her documented role in the text is as a **named witness**: in the Book of Visions (section I.iii), John records testimony from Bridget and a second witness, John of Fontainejean, against the *ars notoria* — that is, both are cited in the text as having independently attested to the art's dangers or falsity, lending external corroboration to John's own visionary conviction that the practice was demonically contaminated (per the Liber florum's own structural reference table, reproduced in *Rewriting Magic*, p.xiv). Beyond this, the precise nature of her involvement — whether she practiced alongside John, received instruction from him, or was simply present to witness and later corroborate his account — is not established in the material read for this portal; that gap is flagged here rather than filled by inference, per this portal's own provenance rule.

The correction of her name is itself informative about the state of Morigny scholarship: even a detail as basic as a named family member's name has shifted across two decades of manuscript work by the field's principal editors, a reminder that the Old/New Compilation textual tradition is still an active, moving target for editorial reconstruction rather than a settled corpus.

figures.name: John of Fontainejean
figures.lifespan: contemporary of John of Morigny, fl. early 14th c.
figures.relation_to_john: fellow witness against the ars notoria
figures.card: Named alongside Bridget/Burgeta in the Book of Visions (section I.iii) as the second of two witnesses whose testimony against the *ars notoria* John of Morigny records in his own text (per the Liber florum's structural reference table, *Rewriting Magic*, p.xiv). Nothing further about his identity, relationship to John, or circumstances is established in the sources read for this portal — he is a real, named figure in John's own account, but essentially unresearched territory beyond that fact.
figures.body:
John of Fontainejean appears in the *Liber florum*'s Book of Visions (I.iii) as one of two named witnesses — the other being John of Morigny's sister, Bridget (Burgeta) — whose testimony against the *ars notoria* John of Morigny incorporates into his own visionary autobiography. This section of the text is described in the Liber florum's own reference table as the "Testimony of two other witnesses against the *ars notoria*" (*Rewriting Magic*, p.xiv), meaning John of Fontainejean's account functioned, alongside Bridget's, as external corroboration for John of Morigny's own conviction that the *ars notoria* was spiritually dangerous or demonically contaminated.

Nothing beyond his name and this structural role is established in the material read for this portal. Whether "Fontainejean" identifies a place of origin, a family name, or a religious house is not resolved here — flagged explicitly rather than guessed, per this portal's provenance rule. A fuller identification would likely require the Fanger–Watson critical edition's own commentary, which was not available to this portal's author at build time.

figures.name: Claire Fanger
figures.card: Professor in the Department of Religion at Rice University (*Rewriting Magic*, p.234). The principal modern scholar of John of Morigny: co-discoverer of a complete New Compilation manuscript in the early 1990s (independently of Sylvie Barnay's parallel find in France), co-editor with Nicholas Watson of the 2015 critical Latin edition of the *Liber florum celestis doctrine* (PIMS), and author of *Rewriting Magic* (Penn State UP, 2015), the first monograph-length study of John. Also editor of *Invoking Angels* (2012) and *Conjuring Spirits* (1998), both collections central to the modern study of medieval ritual magic, and a co-founder of the Societas Magica, the scholarly society for the study of magic in premodern societies. Her reflexive method — writing her own two decades of engagement with John into the scholarship itself — is the explicit model for this portal's own transparency about what is and isn't yet verified.
figures.body: Claire Fanger teaches in the Department of Religion at Rice University (*Rewriting Magic*, p.234, back-matter biography). She is, by a wide margin, the central figure in the modern recovery and study of John of Morigny: her *Rewriting Magic* (2015) is the first and to date only monograph devoted to him, and she is co-editor, with Nicholas Watson, of the critical Latin edition of his *Liber florum celestis doctrine* (Pontifical Institute of Mediaeval Studies, 2015) — the edition on which nearly all detailed factual claims about John ultimately rest. ## Discovery and Two Decades of Work Fanger dates her own engagement with John to "twenty years" of "reading and rereading his words" by the time of *Rewriting Magic*'s writing (*Rewriting Magic*, p.xii — the preface's closing acknowledgment to John himself). The rediscovery of a complete New Compilation manuscript was one of three independent finds converging in the early 1990s: Sylvie Barnay's in France, and Fanger's own, made together with Nicholas Watson in Canada (*Rewriting Magic*, p.21). One version of the origin story that Fanger herself relates: Richard Kieckhefer recalled the *Grandes Chroniques* entry describing the 1323 burning of a Marian-imaged work resembling the *ars notoria*, which set in motion the identification process that led to Watson calling Fanger — "I was the last person Nicholas called" — as the discovery of a matching manuscript was confirmed (*Rewriting Magic*, p.37–39). ## Method *Rewriting Magic*'s preface and introduction are explicit that Fanger considers John a "strong and hardly disinterested collaborator" in the project of representing his own thought — a reflexive, first-person scholarly method in which the historian's own process of coming to understand the subject is narrated alongside the historical argument itself (*Rewriting Magic*, p.xii–xiii). This method is the direct model this portal's own "pencil hand" / apparatus conventions (in the sibling MORIGNYGAME project) are built on — use the method, not the person, per that project's own house rule. ## Other Work and Institutional Role Fanger is also editor of *Invoking Angels: Theurgic Ideas and Practices, Thirteenth to Sixteenth Centuries* (Penn State UP, 2012), a collection in which she contributes both the introduction and a chapter directly on John, "Covenant and the Divine Name: Revisiting the *Liber iuratus* and John of Morigny's *Liber florum*" (p.192), and of *Conjuring Spirits: Texts and Traditions of Medieval Ritual Magic* (Penn State UP, 1998), which contains Nicholas Watson's essay first announcing the modern rediscovery of John's text to the field (per *Rewriting Magic*'s back-matter and cross-references; the *Conjuring Spirits* volume itself was not available to this portal's author — see the *Rewriting Magic* entry in Scholarship for what could be directly verified). She has acknowledged intellectual debts to Sylvie Barnay (credited as "the pioneer in this territory"), and to Frank Klaassen, Benedek Láng, Sophie Page, and Julien Véronèse as ongoing points of reference (*Rewriting Magic*, p.xi). ## Literature - Fanger, Claire. *Rewriting Magic*. figures.body:
Nicholas Watson is Claire Fanger's collaborator on the critical Latin edition of John of Morigny's *Liber florum celestis doctrine* (Pontifical Institute of Mediaeval Studies, 2015), and co-discoverer with her of a complete New Compilation manuscript in Canada in the early 1990s — a find made independently of, and roughly contemporaneous with, Sylvie Barnay's separate discovery in France (*Rewriting Magic*, p.21). Fanger's preface to *Rewriting Magic* describes him as "longtime friend, reader, listener, and sparring partner, who in many ways — some more annoying than others — always pushed me to read more deeply, see more clearly, learn more thoroughly, and write more accurately," adding that the book "would not have been possible without him" (*Rewriting Magic*, p.xiii).

Watson wrote "John the Monk's *Book of Visions of the Blessed and Undefiled Virgin Mary, Mother of God*: Two Anonymous Reworkings, and Oswald de Corda," the essay in Fanger's edited *Conjuring Spirits* (Penn State UP, 1998) that first announced the modern rediscovery of John's text to the scholarly field — this essay itself was not available to this portal's author, so its specific claims are cited here only by title, via *Rewriting Magic*'s own cross-references, and not independently verified.

Watson also authored "Introduction A" to the Fanger–Watson critical edition, which Fanger's 2015 preface cites directly for background on John's likely location at Orléans (*Rewriting Magic*, p.xi, note to §8) — confirming Watson's role in the edition extends to substantial original biographical and contextual argument, not just textual apparatus.

This portal's author was not able to confirm Watson's specific institutional affiliation from the sources read; general scholarly reputation places him at Harvard University, but that detail is deliberately left unstated in the card above pending direct confirmation, per this portal's confidence discipline.

figures.name: Richard Kieckhefer
figures.region: Northwestern University (per standard scholarly attribution; not independently confirmed in the corpus read for this portal)
figures.relation_to_john: helped set the 1990s rediscovery in motion; longtime reader of Fanger's work
figures.card: Author of *Magic in the Middle Ages* (1989) and *Forbidden Rites: A Necromancer's Manual of the Fifteenth Century* (1997), foundational studies that established much of the modern field's vocabulary and periodization for medieval ritual magic — including the phrase "clerical underworld" for the milieu of student and clerical necromancy John himself passed through at Orléans. Fanger's preface credits him with recalling the *Grandes Chroniques* entry on the 1323 burning that helped set the rediscovery process in motion, and thanks him for "sustained interest in my work over the years" and for reading the *Rewriting Magic* manuscript in draft (*Rewriting Magic*, p.xii).
figures.body:
Richard Kieckhefer's *Magic in the Middle Ages* (Cambridge University Press, 1989; Canto Classics ed. 2014) is one of the two or three most cited general studies of medieval magic in the field, and his *Forbidden Rites: A Necromancer's Manual of the Fifteenth Century* (Penn State UP / Sutton, 1997) an equally standard close study of a single necromantic manuscript. His phrase for the milieu of student and clerical experimentation with forbidden ritual texts — the "clerical underworld" — has become standard shorthand across the field for exactly the world John of Morigny passed through as a young canon-law student at Orléans.

Kieckhefer has a direct, personal role in the story of John's modern rediscovery: per Fanger's own account in *Rewriting Magic*, "Richard remembered the entry in the *Grandes Chroniques* describing the 1323 burning of a work by a French monk, like an *ars notoria*, but with Marian images in it," a recollection that set in motion the identification process eventually connecting a newly found manuscript to the historical John (*Rewriting Magic*, p.37). Fanger's preface separately thanks him "for reading and responding to the initial manuscript draft of *Rewriting Magic*, as well as for his sustained interest in my work over the years" (*Rewriting Magic*, p.xii).

His 1994 *American Historical Review* article "The Specific Rationality of Medieval Magic" and his general study *Magic in the Middle Ages* are both part of the corpus this portal draws on for context; neither is a work about John specifically, but both establish the intellectual framework (magic as a coherent, rule-governed practice rather than mere superstition) within which John's own project of purifying and re-authorizing a condemned ritual art becomes historically legible rather than simply anomalous.

This portal's author was not able to independently confirm Kieckhefer's institutional affiliation from the corpus read; he is generally attributed to Northwestern University in the wider field, but that detail is left unconfirmed here per this portal's confidence discipline.

figures.name: Julien Véronèse
figures.region: not confirmed in sources read for this portal
figures.relation_to_john: leading modern scholar of the ars notoria tradition John practiced
figures.card: The leading modern scholar of the *ars notoria* text tradition — the ritual system John of Morigny practiced before rewriting it — and, per Fanger's preface, one of her ongoing points of reference (*Rewriting Magic*, p.xi). His essay "Magic, Theurgy, and Spirituality in the Medieval Ritual of the *Ars notoria*," translated into English by Fanger herself, opens Fanger's edited volume *Invoking Angels* (2012), p.37 — making his own scholarship, otherwise published mainly in French and not independently held in this portal's corpus, directly readable here in translation.
figures.body:
Julien Véronèse is the field's leading specialist on the *ars notoria* as a ritual and textual tradition in its own right — the specific art of prayer, figure-contemplation, and *verba ignota* (unknown words) that John of Morigny practiced as a young man before coming to regard it as demonically contaminated and rewriting it into the *Liber florum*. Fanger's preface to *Rewriting Magic* names him among the colleagues whose "writings remain an ongoing point of reference for my own work," alongside Frank Klaassen, Benedek Láng, and Sophie Page (*Rewriting Magic*, p.xi).

Véronèse's standalone monographs and critical editions of the *ars notoria* corpus (published primarily in French) were not available to this portal's author. However, his essay "Magic, Theurgy, and Spirituality in the Medieval Ritual of the *Ars notoria*" — translated into English by Fanger herself — opens her edited volume *Invoking Angels: Theurgic Ideas and Practices, Thirteenth to Sixteenth Centuries* (Penn State UP, 2012), beginning at p.37. This chapter makes his own direct scholarly voice on the *ars notoria* tradition readable within this portal's corpus, even where his French-language monographs remain out of reach — a genuine, if partial, closing of what would otherwise be a real gap in this portal's source access. See [[ars-notoria]] for the concept entry this essay substantially informs.

concepts.name: Ars Notoria
concepts.literal_meaning: the notable/notorious art; sometimes glossed "the art of rapid learning"
concepts.card: A ritual system, attested in over fifty manuscripts across western Europe by Véronèse's count, promising infused knowledge of the liberal arts, philosophy, and theology through prayer and the contemplation of geometric figures (*notae*) inscribed with angelic names and prayers. Its own founding myth holds the art was revealed by God to Adam, then to Solomon via the angel Pamphilius, inscribed on golden tables (*tabulae aureae*). Condemned by name by Thomas Aquinas and other scholastic authorities, yet never effectively suppressed — Véronèse reads its persistence as evidence of genuine institutional ambivalence about its status, not merely failed policing. John of Morigny practiced it as a young monk at Orléans before rewriting it as the *Liber florum*.
concepts.body:
The *ars notoria* is a ritual system for obtaining infused divine knowledge of the liberal arts, philosophy, and theology — not through study, but through a program of prayer, fasting, and the contemplation of geometric diagrams called *notae*, each inscribed with prayers and lists of angelic names (Véronèse, in Fanger, ed., *Invoking Angels*, p.44). It survives, per Véronèse's count, in more than fifty manuscripts scattered across western European and North American libraries — a manuscript base he explicitly reads as evidence that ritual magic "was not a marginal element in the cultural world of the literate elite" (*Invoking Angels*, p.41).

## Textual Structure

Every complete text of the notory art contains two core elements: the *Flores aurei* ("Golden Flowers") and the *Ars nova* ("New Art"). Manuscripts fall into two textual stages: an older, thirteenth-century (or possibly late twelfth-century) base version giving the ritual's large structure without enough operational detail for a postulant lacking a master to actually perform it; and a later, heavily glossed version from the late thirteenth century onward, in which a substantial marginal commentary — in the manuscript Véronèse uses as his reference text, BnF Latin 9336, the gloss makes up as much as 43–57% of the whole content depending on how the figure-texts themselves are counted — supplies the operational instructions the base text lacks (*Invoking Angels*, p.42–43). This BnF Latin 9336 manuscript is the same 13th-century French manuscript from which this portal's sibling project, MORIGNYGAME, has sourced an image ("the first figure of grammar") — a direct point of contact between this portal's scholarship and that project's art direction.

## The Founding Myth

The art's own prologue narrates its origin: God gave humankind, at creation, a natural aptitude for knowledge; the *ars notoria* does nothing but improve on that God-given faculty, and so cannot work against the divine plan. It was first delivered to Adam, and later to Solomon, who received the *tabulae aureae* — golden tables inscribed with the angelic names and prayers constituting the art — from the hands of the angel Pamphilius, "the principal minister of God." A second authority, Apollonius ("the philosopher"), is credited as the art's great disseminator among later practitioners (*Invoking Angels*, p.43). This Adam-then-Solomon transmission myth recurs, with variations, throughout the treatise's glossed commentary.

## Condemnation and Persistence

The *ars notoria* was condemned by name by Alexander of Hales, Thomas Aquinas, and other scholastic doctors of the Church (*Invoking Angels*, p.41). Véronèse poses the genuinely open historiographical question of what its wide, sustained manuscript survival despite this condemnation actually means: either the condemnation was simply ineffective against a practice already too embedded in clerical literate culture, or — the reading he leans toward, by comparison with the more clearly demonic and more actively suppressed practice of "nigromancy" — its persistence reflects a real and sustained institutional ambivalence about its actual status, since (following Aquinas's own hesitation) its objective nature was genuinely more ambiguous than necromancy's (*Invoking Angels*, p.41). See [[censorship-does-not-work]] for the closely related argument Fanger makes about the *Liber florum*'s own post-condemnation survival.

## John of Morigny's Relation to It

John practiced the *ars notoria* as a young monk, almost certainly at Orléans, before a sequence of visions convinced him it was demonically contaminated (see [[john-of-morigny]], and [[timeline-vision-9]] for the decisive episode). His response was not abandonment but rewriting: the *Liber florum celestis doctrine* is explicitly structured to imitate the ars notoria's own shape — prayers, figures, a promise of infused knowledge — while claiming its authorization directly from the Virgin Mary rather than from Solomon and Pamphilius, and while explicitly invoking the Augustinian trope of "plunder[ing]" the old art's own "sacred and divine words... as the Hebrews plundered the Egyptian treasure" (Fanger, *Rewriting Magic*, p.2; see [[plundering-egyptian-treasure]]). Fanger has published a structural comparison of John's *Liber visionum* against the ars notoria treatise tradition, cited by Véronèse but not independently read for this portal (*Invoking Angels*, p.43–44, citing Fanger's article).

concepts.name: Notae
concepts.card: The geometric figures at the heart of both the *ars notoria* and John of Morigny's own *Liber florum*: diagrams inscribed with prayers and angelic names, meant to be contemplated (not merely read) as part of the ritual's operation. In the *ars notoria* tradition, texts inserted into the *notae* could run to roughly a quarter of a full treatise's content by Véronèse's count. John's own Book of Figures — condemned once in 1315 and rewritten as part of the New Compilation — is built around a parallel set of figures whose fidelity to the correct geometric form was held to determine the efficacy of the whole operation.
concepts.body:
*Notae* — geometric figures inscribed with prayers and lists of angelic names, meant to be gazed upon as part of a ritual operation rather than simply read — are structurally central to both the *ars notoria* John of Morigny practiced as a young man and the *Liber florum celestis doctrine* he later composed to replace it. In Julien Véronèse's analysis of the *ars notoria* tradition (BnF Latin 9336 as reference manuscript), the textual material inscribed directly into the *notae* — as distinct from the treatise's main prayers and its glossed commentary — makes up roughly 27% of the whole manuscript's content, a substantial share of the work in its own right (Véronèse, in Fanger, ed., *Invoking Angels*, p.43).

John's own Book of Figures (Part III of the *Liber florum*) is the direct heir to this tradition. Per the *Liber florum*'s own structural table, its New Compilation version narrates "visions of revelation of the seven figures" before describing them so operators can execute a Second Procedure ritual with them, and separately narrates the "revelation of the ring" — instructions for a ring to be worn by the operator on special occasions, associated with what the text occasionally calls a Third Procedure (*Rewriting Magic*, p.xv–xvi).

The stakes of getting a *nota*'s geometry exactly right were understood, in this tradition, as more than aesthetic: fidelity of the figure to its correct form was bound up with the efficacy of the whole operation it supported — an inaccurately copied figure risked invalidating the ritual it was meant to enable. This is the historical basis for treating figure-copying as a distinct, high-stakes skill within manuscript production of these texts, separate from ordinary textual copying.

concepts.name: "Plundering the Egyptian Treasure"
concepts.literal_meaning: a biblical trope (Exodus 12:35–36; developed by Augustine) justifying the extraction of good material from a corrupted or pagan source
concepts.card: The biblical-exegetical trope John of Morigny explicitly invokes to justify his own project: taking the *ars notoria*'s "sacred and divine words" and repurposing them for the *Liber florum*, "as the Hebrews plundered the Egyptian treasure" — an allusion to Exodus 12:35–36, developed by Augustine as a justification for Christians extracting true or useful material from pagan learning. For John, it licenses rewriting a condemned ritual art rather than discarding it wholesale, and frames his whole project as recovery and purification rather than invention.
concepts.body:
When John of Morigny explains, in the Book of Visions, why he felt entitled to draw on the language and structure of the condemned *ars notoria* for his own *Liber florum*, he reaches for a specific, well-established biblical trope: he "explicitly plunders the ars notoria, pulling its 'sacred and divine words' into his own book 'as the Hebrews plundered the Egyptian treasure'" (Fanger, *Rewriting Magic*, p.2).

The allusion is to Exodus 12:35–36, where the Israelites, departing Egypt, are described as having despoiled the Egyptians of gold, silver, and clothing at God's own prompting. Augustine of Hippo developed this passage into a durable exegetical justification for Christian use of pagan learning: just as the Israelites took Egyptian gold and put it to a better, sanctified use, Christian scholars may extract true or useful material from non-Christian or otherwise suspect sources without thereby endorsing those sources' errors. Fanger identifies John's own use of the trope as directly in this Augustinian line.

The trope does real conceptual work for John's project. It allows him to treat the *ars notoria*'s prayers and structure as raw material that was never wholly bad — gold, not dross — while still maintaining that the *ars notoria* itself, as a complete system, was demonically contaminated and rightly condemned. This is the same move that lets John rewrite rather than simply abandon ritual practice after each condemnation (1315 and 1323): the underlying premise that structured prayer can licitly obtain divine knowledge survives even as the specific vehicle for it is repeatedly purified and re-authorized. See [[ars-notoria]] and [[old-new-compilation]].

concepts.name: Old Compilation / New Compilation
concepts.literal_meaning: John's own two major redactions of the Liber florum
concepts.card: John of Morigny's two major redactions of his own book. The Old Compilation was itself already revised at least once before 1315; the **New Compilation** was written in direct, urgent response to the 1315 condemnation of the original Book of Figures by unnamed "Barking Dogs," offering an alternative ritual and spiritual process rather than simply defending the old one. Of the twenty-three known manuscripts (as of Fanger's 2015 count), only one preserves the Old Compilation; eighteen preserve all or substantial portions of the New.
concepts.body:
John of Morigny's *Liber florum celestis doctrine* survives in two major authorial redactions, referred to in the scholarship as the Old Compilation and the New Compilation.

Internal textual evidence — successive strata visible across the prayers and the Book of Visions — shows the Old Compilation had already been revised at least once even before the 1315 condemnation (Fanger, *Rewriting Magic*, p.118): John was a habitual reviser of his own work well before institutional pressure forced a more drastic rewrite. The **New Compilation** proper, however, is a direct and urgent response to that 1315 condemnation of the original Book of Figures by unnamed "Barking Dogs" (canon lawyers) who judged its figures too close to necromantic diagrams. Because the condemned Old Book of Figures had already circulated to a community of operators, John could not simply recall it; instead he composed, "in great haste," a new installment offering an alternative model for the same ritual and spiritual process, leaning more heavily than before on direct visionary authorization from the Virgin (*Rewriting Magic*, p.2–3).

Of the twenty-three manuscripts known to Fanger as of her 2015 count, the great majority preserve the New Compilation: eighteen contain all or substantial portions of it, against just one manuscript preserving the Old Compilation, plus four further manuscripts that are prayer-collections drawing unattributed sequences from the work (*Rewriting Magic*, p.xi). This lopsided survival is itself informative — whatever readership the *Liber florum* found across its two centuries of circulation, it found overwhelmingly through the New, post-condemnation version of the text, not the version John first wrote.

The New Compilation's own Book of Figures (NC III.i) explicitly describes the 1315 attack, makes specific corrections to the Old Book of Figures, and outlines a simplified Second Procedure for using the figures with the prayers (per the *Liber florum*'s own structural reference table, *Rewriting Magic*, p.xv).

concepts.name: "Barking Dogs"
concepts.literal_meaning: John's own term for his unnamed 1315 condemners
concepts.card: John of Morigny's own term for the unnamed condemners who, in 1315, judged his original Book of Figures too closely resembled necromantic diagrams — a condemnation distinct from and eight years earlier than the famous 1323 Paris burning. They "must have had professional knowledge of canon law," per Fanger, but are never further identified in the text. concepts.body:
"Barking Dogs" is John of Morigny's own phrase — never further explained in the surviving text — for the unnamed figures who, in 1315, condemned his original Book of Figures on the grounds that its figures too closely resembled necromantic diagrams. This is a real, textually distinct condemnation, separate from and eight years before the famous 1323 Paris burning recorded in the *Grandes Chroniques de France* (see [[condemnation-1315]] and [[condemnation-1323]]). Fanger judges that the condemners "must have had professional knowledge of canon law," given the nature of the objection, though the text never names them (*Rewriting Magic*, p.2).

A notable historiographical correction: Fanger's own earlier published work had placed the Barking Dogs' activity at **Sens**, the archiepiscopal see with jurisdiction over the region. Her 2015 preface to *Rewriting Magic* explicitly retracts this: "the provenance of the 'Barking Dogs' who condemned John's work in 1315 is no longer securely located at Sens, where I placed it in publications after 2001. Our original manuscript reading for this place name turned out to be in error. While other noteworthy condemnations originated in Sens in this time period, this is only one possible point of origin, and cannot now be nailed to textual evidence" (*Rewriting Magic*, p.x). This is a live example of exactly the kind of correction ongoing manuscript work on the *Liber florum* keeps producing — a fact this portal's own "Findings already in hand" methodology treats as a feature of the field's current state, not an embarrassment to smooth over.

The 1315 condemnation is what directly produced the New Compilation: unable to recall an already-circulating condemned text, John instead composed a rewritten Book of Figures offering an alternative ritual process (see [[old-new-compilation]]).

texts.title: Liber florum celestis doctrine
texts.date_or_period: composed in installments, early 14th c.; New Compilation written urgently after 1315
texts.card: John of Morigny's own book, composed in installments over many years and circulated to an expanding community of ritual operators: a purified prayer-and-vision system explicitly modeled on the *ars notoria* but claiming direct authorization from the Virgin Mary. Breaks into three parts — the Book of Visions (autobiography and apologia), the Book of Prayers (the ritual liturgy, culminating in the First Procedure), and the Book of Figures (further visions and diagrams, the Second and Third Procedures). Condemned in 1315 and burned at Paris in 1323, it nonetheless survives in twenty-three known manuscripts and was the primary vehicle for the *ars notoria*'s own after-life among literate monks for two centuries.
texts.body:
The *Liber florum celestis doctrine* ("Book/Flowers of Heavenly Teaching") is the one extant work through which modern scholarship has access to John of Morigny. Fanger describes it as "a complicated and polyvalent work that John wrote in installments and circulated to an expanding audience of ritual operators over many years" (*Rewriting Magic*, p.1). Until recently there were no printed editions; the text remained effectively unknown and inaccessible from the early sixteenth century until its rediscovery in the early 1990s.

## Structure

The finished work breaks into three principal parts, per its own internal structure (reproduced in Fanger, *Rewriting Magic*, p.xiv–xvi):

- **I. Book of Visions** — a visionary autobiography and apologia: a General Prologue, a Prologue to the Book of Visions, an account of visions induced by the *ars notoria* (I.i), good visions received after John laid the *ars notoria* aside (I.ii), the testimony of two named witnesses against the *ars notoria* — Bridget/Burgeta and John of Fontainejean (I.iii) — and preparations for the Book of Prayers (I.iv), including an exhortation on right intention and criteria for distinguishing true from false visions of Mary.
- **II. Book of Prayers** — a lengthy liturgy addressed to God and the angels for the infusion of divine and curricular knowledge, structured as Seven Prayers (an Acquisitional opus, requesting permission to proceed) followed by Thirty Prayers organized into further *opera* — Auxiliative, Preparative, General Executive, Special Executive for the liberal arts, for philosophy, and for theology, and a concluding thanksgiving — culminating in the **First Procedure**, a ritual manual for using the prayers.
- **III. Book of Figures** — further visions and a set of *notae* designed to work with and enhance the ritual process (the operations of which are sometimes called the "Second Procedure"), including, in some manuscript traditions, a "Third Procedure" involving a consecrated ring.

## Content and Claims

In the Book of Visions, John confesses to earlier experimentation with both necromancy and the *ars notoria*; his own Book of Prayers is explicitly structured to imitate the shape of the art he came to regard as demonically contaminated (*Rewriting Magic*, p.2). The whole work simultaneously records the process of its own composition under the guidance of the Virgin Mary — its prayers, visualizations, and figures are designed to enable the same kind of visionary communication with Mary, Christ, and the angels that John records himself experiencing.

## Condemnation and Rewriting

Composition was interrupted twice: a 1315 condemnation of the original Book of Figures by unnamed "Barking Dogs" (see [[barking-dogs]]), and the far more famous 1323 burning at Paris recorded in the *Grandes Chroniques de France* (see [[condemnation-1323]]). The first produced the New Compilation (see [[old-new-compilation]]); John's response to the second is not detailed in the sources read for this portal.

## Manuscript Survival

As of Fanger's 2015 count, twenty-three manuscripts contain all or part of the work: one with the Old Compilation, eighteen with all or substantial portions of the New Compilation, and four prayer-collections drawing unattributed sequences from it (*Rewriting Magic*, p.xi). Fanger argues this post-1323 survival directly challenges the assumption that public book-burning constitutes effective censorship (see [[censorship-does-not-work]]).

texts.title: Grandes Chroniques de France, entry for 1323
texts.title_translated: the first extended notice of John's condemnation
texts.card: The first extended modern-accessible notice of John's condemnation: an entry for the year 1323 in the *Grandes Chroniques de France* recording that an unnamed "monk of Morigny" had wanted to "inspire and renew a condemned heresy and sorcery called in Latin *ars notoria*," describing a book of Marian images promising all knowledge and "any riches, honours or pleasures one wanted to have," declared "false and evil... and condemned to be burned and put on the fire." The single surviving thread connecting John to modern scholarship for over six centuries, and the origin point of a long chain of increasingly garbled later paraphrases.
texts.body:
The *Grandes Chroniques de France* contains, under the year 1323, the first extended notice of the condemnation of an unnamed "monk of Morigny." The entry states the monk had wanted to "inspire and renew a condemned heresy and sorcery called in Latin *ars notoria*," describing the art in terms conventional for the period — a science bestowing different branches of knowledge when its figures were contemplated with fasting and prayer, involving the invocation of "little known names which were firmly believed to be the names of demons." The chronicle further records that the monk, who himself condemned the *ars notoria*, had nonetheless compiled a book full of images in honor of the Virgin, whose use procured for the operator not only all branches of knowledge but "any riches, honours or pleasures one wanted to have." The book is declared "false and evil, against the Christian faith, and condemned to be burned and put on the fire" (Fanger, *Rewriting Magic*, p.3, quoting/paraphrasing the chronicle).

Fanger judges aspects of this account "inaccurate, if not unfair" to the actual text — the *Liber florum* is explicitly not concerned with earthly riches or pleasures — but notes it at least correctly distinguishes John's book from the *ars notoria* itself, a distinction that subsequent paraphrases across the centuries steadily lost (see [[historiography-of-erasure]]).

This single chronicle entry was, for over six hundred years, the *only* trace of John of Morigny available to any reader — the *Liber florum* itself had vanished from view entirely — making this text the true origin point of everything the field now knows, or thought it knew, about him before the 1990s manuscript rediscoveries.

texts.title: Chronicle of Guillaume de Nangis (continuation)
texts.title_translated: the Latin chronicle tradition's own version of the 1323 notice
texts.card: The continuation of Guillaume de Nangis's Latin chronicle of the kings of France — a distinct textual witness from the vernacular Grandes Chroniques de France, part of the same Saint-Denis chronicle tradition — carries its own, more compressed version of the 1323 condemnation notice. Fanger identifies this compression as the second link (after the original Grandes Chroniques entry) in the chain of paraphrase that eventually strips John of authorship of his own book by the time of Henry Charles Lea's 1887 history.
texts.body:
## Overview

Guillaume de Nangis (d. 1300) was a monk of Saint-Denis whose Latin chronicle of the kings of France was continued by later anonymous hands into the fourteenth century; this continuation tradition runs in close parallel to, but is textually distinct from, the vernacular *Grandes Chroniques de France* that first records the 1323 condemnation of the unnamed "monk of Morigny" (see [[grandes-chroniques-1323-notice]]).

## Role in the Historiography of Erasure

Fanger identifies the Nangis continuation's retelling of the 1323 notice as a further compression of the original account — not yet the outright misattribution that would follow in the sixteenth century (see [[timeline-antiquitez-de-paris-16thc]]), but an early step in the same direction: less specific, less careful about the distinction between John's own book and the *ars notoria* tradition it drew on (*Rewriting Magic*, p.3, p.20). This portal has not independently read the Nangis continuation's own Latin text; its content here is described only as Fanger characterizes it.

institutions.name: Abbey of Morigny
institutions.period: medieval; John's home house, early 14th c.
institutions.card: The Benedictine abbey near Étampes to which John was attached as monk and priest — the source of his identifying name. Beyond this basic fact of affiliation, the sources read for this portal do not treat the abbey's own institutional history in detail; that remains outside this portal's Phase 1 scope.

institutions.name: University of Orléans
institutions.period: medieval; John's period of study, early 14th c.
institutions.card: Where John earned his advanced degree in canon law — one of only two university subjects open to a professed monk (the other, theology, being restricted to Paris). Fanger's 2015 preface newly identifies Orléans, not her own earlier guess of Chartres, as the far more likely site of John's *ars notoria* experiments, given his documented presence there as a student and the university's specialization in law.
institutions.body:
The University of Orléans specialized in civil and canon law, and was, alongside Paris (theology), one of only two university venues open to a professed monk like John of Morigny for advanced study (Fanger, *Rewriting Magic*, p.x–xi). John's own text confirms he studied there. Fanger's 2015 preface explicitly corrects her own earlier published suggestion that his *ars notoria* experiments took place at Chartres; the balance of evidence — his documented presence at Orléans as a canon-law student, and the fact that his own text shows him "rubbing shoulders with friars and Cistercians" there while also visiting his sister nearby — now points to Orléans as the far more probable site (*Rewriting Magic*, p.x–xi).

Orléans, per the wider field's standard characterization (Kieckhefer's phrase, adopted broadly), sat within reach of the "clerical underworld" of student and clerical necromancy — the milieu in which forbidden ritual texts like the *ars notoria* and outright necromantic manuals circulated among literate clerics with university access. John's own confessed experimentation with both the *ars notoria* and *nigromancia* places him squarely within this world during his Orléans years.

timeline_events.title: John studies canon law at Orléans; ars notoria experiments
timeline_events.card: As a young, already-professed monk, John pursues advanced study at the University of Orléans — one of only two university subjects (with Paris theology) open to a monk. It is almost certainly here, not at Chartres as Fanger's own earlier work once suggested, that he first experiments with the *ars notoria* and, by his own later confession, with necromancy (*nigromancia*) too.

timeline_events.title: The decisive vision: John turns from the ars notoria
timeline_events.card: A sequence of visions — including a penitential vision of Christ recorded in the Book of Visions — convinces John his ars notoria practice was demonically contaminated. The two witnesses he names, Bridget (Burgeta) and John of Fontainejean, testify to related experiences at roughly this period. This is the pivot from ars notoria practitioner to author of a purified replacement: the germ of the *Liber florum*.

timeline_events.title: Old Compilation composed and circulated
timeline_events.card: John writes the first full version of the *Liber florum celestis doctrine* — the Old Compilation — in installments, and circulates it to a growing community of ritual operators. Internal textual strata show he had already revised it at least once even before external condemnation forced the more drastic 1315 rewrite.

timeline_events.title: 1315: The "Barking Dogs" condemn the Book of Figures
timeline_events.place: unlocated — Fanger's earlier "Sens" attribution now retracted
timeline_events.card: Unnamed canon lawyers — John's own term for them, never explained further — condemn his original Book of Figures as too closely resembling necromantic diagrams. This is a real, distinct condemnation eight years before the famous 1323 Paris burning, and the direct cause of the New Compilation: John cannot recall the already-circulating condemned text, so instead rewrites the ritual and spiritual process it describes.

timeline_events.title: New Compilation written in haste
timeline_events.card: In direct, urgent response to the 1315 condemnation, John composes a rewritten Book of Figures — and, with it, a revised Book of Visions describing the attack itself — leaning more heavily on direct visionary authorization from the Virgin than the Old Compilation had. This New Compilation becomes the version that dominates the manuscript record: 18 of 23 known manuscripts preserve all or substantial portions of it, against just one for the Old Compilation.

timeline_events.title: 1323: The Liber florum burned at Paris
timeline_events.card: The *Grandes Chroniques de France* records, for this year, the condemnation of an unnamed "monk of Morigny" for compiling a book of Marian images promising all knowledge and worldly reward — judged "false and evil... condemned to be burned and put on the fire." For over six centuries this chronicle notice was the only trace of John of Morigny available to any reader; the *Liber florum* itself had vanished from view.

timeline_events.title: Post-1323: continued manuscript transmission
timeline_events.place: northern French and neighboring monastic houses, likely via Benedictine travel
timeline_events.card: Despite the Paris burning, the *Liber florum* continued to be copied and used among literate monks for roughly two centuries — evidence Fanger reads as directly challenging the assumption that a public book-burning constitutes effective censorship. See [[censorship-does-not-work]].

timeline_events.title: The long silence: John vanishes from view
timeline_events.card: Following the last known manuscript copying activity, John of Morigny effectively disappears from scholarship for roughly four centuries, known — if at all — only through a chain of increasingly garbled paraphrases of the 1323 chronicle notice: a 16th-century Parisian antiquarian history that falsely credits him with *inventing* the ars notoria, then Henry Charles Lea's 1887 history of the Inquisition, which strips him of authorship of his own book entirely.

timeline_events.title: 1987: Jean Dupèbe notices a Munich manuscript
timeline_events.card: Jean Dupèbe's 1987 notice of a Munich manuscript is the first modern scholarly flag that a text by John of Morigny actually survives, independent of the chronicle paraphrase chain — the opening move in the rediscovery that would culminate in the 1990s.

timeline_events.title: 1990s: the Kieckhefer–Watson–Fanger rediscovery
timeline_events.card: Building on Dupèbe's notice and Sylvie Barnay's own pioneering work (credited by Fanger as foundational, though not independently detailed as a figure entry in this Phase 1 build), Richard Kieckhefer, Nicholas Watson, and Claire Fanger together drive the modern rediscovery and identification of the *Liber florum* across the 1990s — the beginning of the field that now exists around John of Morigny.

timeline_events.title: 2015: the Fanger–Watson critical edition and Rewriting Magic
timeline_events.card: Claire Fanger and Nicholas Watson publish the first critical edition of the *Liber florum celestis doctrine* (PIMS), and Fanger publishes *Rewriting Magic* (Penn State), her own monograph-length study — together the modern foundation this portal itself draws on most directly.

timeline_events.title: Vision 8: a first, incomplete rejection
timeline_events.card: Before the decisive Vision 9, John's Book of Visions records an earlier vision (Vision 8) in which God expresses unambiguous prohibition of the ars notoria. John's own conversion is not sudden: he records that he "put it away from me somewhat, but not entirely" (Rewriting Magic, p.66, Fanger quoting the Book of Visions directly) — a false start Fanger reads as evidence the text is a genuine confessio, not a smoothed hagiographic narrative.

timeline_events.title: Guillaume de Nangis's chronicle compresses the 1323 account
timeline_events.card: The continuation of Guillaume de Nangis's Latin chronicle — a distinct textual witness from the vernacular Grandes Chroniques de France — retells the 1323 condemnation in compressed form, the first step in the centuries-long chain of paraphrase that Fanger traces from a roughly accurate original notice toward the near-total erasure of John's authorship. See the Grandes Chroniques 1323 notice for the fuller original account, and The historiography of erasure for the whole chain.

timeline_events.title: A 16th-century Parisian antiquarian history inverts the record
timeline_events.card: A sixteenth-century antiquarian history of Paris (cited in Fanger's own historiographical account as Antiquitez... de Paris) takes the erasure a step further than Nangis's compression: it falsely credits the unnamed "monk of Morigny" with having invented the ars notoria itself, collapsing the distinction between John's own book and the older tradition he drew on and rewrote — a distinction the original 1323 Grandes Chroniques notice had actually preserved.

timeline_events.title: 1887: Henry Charles Lea erases John as author
timeline_events.card: Henry Charles Lea's A History of the Inquisition of the Middle Ages (1887), drawing on the already-degraded chain of paraphrase running from the Grandes Chroniques through Nangis's compression to the 16th-century Antiquitez... de Paris, removes John as an identifiable author of the condemned book altogether — the low point of the historiography of erasure, and the last major secondary reference to the case before Jean Dupèbe's 1987 manuscript notice began the modern recovery.

timeline_events.title: 1998: Nicholas Watson's essay announces the rediscovery to the field
timeline_events.card: Nicholas Watson's essay "John the Monk's Book of Visions of the Blessed and Undefiled Virgin Mary, Mother of God: Two Anonymous Reworkings, and Oswald de Corda," published in Claire Fanger's edited volume Conjuring Spirits: Texts and Traditions of Medieval Ritual Magic (Penn State University Press, 1998), is the essay that first announces the modern manuscript rediscovery to the field of medieval-magic scholarship — the earliest point at which John of Morigny's own text, rather than the degraded chronicle-paraphrase chain, becomes available for study again. The essay itself was not available on this portal's machine and is cited here only from Fanger's own back-matter cross-references in Rewriting Magic, not independently read.

timeline_events.title: 2001: Fanger and Watson publish the Liber Visionum prologue
timeline_events.card: Claire Fanger and Nicholas Watson publish "The Prologue to John of Morigny's Liber Visionum: Text and Translation" in Esoterica 3 (2001) — the first substantial English-language scholarship on the text. This article is also the origin of two claims Fanger's own 2015 preface to Rewriting Magic later retracts as manuscript-reading errors: the location of John's ars notoria experiments at Chartres (corrected to Orléans) and the location of the 1315 "Barking Dogs" condemnation at Sens (retracted as unlocatable on present textual evidence) — a documented instance of the field's understanding self-correcting on further manuscript work, not a single fixed picture.

arguments.title: Book condemnation is not effective censorship
arguments.claim: The Liber florum's continued transmission and ritual use among literate monks after the 1323 Paris burning directly challenges the widespread assumption that a public book-burning effectively suppresses a text.
arguments.against: the intuitive, commonly assumed equivalence between a recorded condemnation/burning and actual textual suppression
arguments.evidence: Eighteen of twenty-three known manuscripts preserve the New Compilation, produced and copied well after 1323, likely spread via Benedictine inter-monastic travel; the text's own "afterlife" in continued use is itself the evidence.
arguments.stakes: Reframes how historians should read every other recorded medieval book-burning as evidence of suppression's intent, not its success — a methodological caution against reading condemnation notices as if they settle a text's actual fate.
arguments.card: Fanger argues, against the intuitive assumption that a 1323 public burning would have suppressed a text, that the evidence of the *Liber florum*'s continued transmission and ritual use among literate monks *after* 1323 — likely via Benedictine travel between monasteries — directly challenges "the widespread belief that book condemnation constitutes effective censorship" (*Rewriting Magic*, p.21–22). Stakes: reframes how historians should read every other recorded medieval book-burning as evidence of suppression's *intent*, not its success.
arguments.body:
## The argument, precisely

Fanger argues that the historical record of the *Liber florum celestis doctrine*'s manuscript transmission — the great majority of surviving copies dating from after the 1323 Paris condemnation and burning — is direct evidence against a common historiographical assumption: that a recorded public book-burning effectively ended a text's circulation and use.

## Against what

The assumption under challenge is widespread enough that it usually goes unstated: when a chronicle records a book burned as heretical or dangerous, historians have tended to treat the text's practical history as over at that point, its condemnation and its disappearance from use treated as more or less the same event.

## Evidence

Of the twenty-three manuscripts of the *Liber florum* known to Fanger as of her 2015 count, eighteen preserve all or substantial portions of the New Compilation — the version John completed years before 1323, meaning its post-1323 copies represent genuine continued transmission, not merely survivals predating the burning. Fanger attributes this ongoing circulation most plausibly to travel between Benedictine houses, the same institutional network that had originally connected John's own community to its wider monastic world (*Rewriting Magic*, p.21–22).

## Reception

This argument is presented within Fanger's own monograph as a framing claim for why the *Liber florum*'s history matters beyond antiquarian interest in one obscure monk — it is offered as a caution applicable to how historians read condemnation notices generally, not only in John's specific case. This portal has not independently verified how the wider field has taken up or contested this specific framing beyond Fanger's own book.

## Literature

- Fanger, Claire. *Rewriting Magic*. Penn State University Press, 2015, p.21–22.

arguments.title: Rewriting is devotion, not retraction
arguments.claim: John's repeated response to condemnation — rewriting the ritual and its textual vehicle rather than abandoning ritual practice altogether — should be read as an act of ongoing devotional labor, continuous with his visionary project, not as a forced retreat or a merely defensive maneuver.
arguments.against: a reading that would treat the New Compilation as simply a chastened, defanged replacement produced under duress
arguments.evidence: The New Compilation leans more heavily, not less, on direct visionary authorization from the Virgin than the Old Compilation had; John frames the whole project, across both compilations, using the Augustinian trope of plundering the Egyptian treasure — extracting what is genuinely sacred from a corrupted vehicle, a constructive rather than merely defensive stance.
arguments.stakes: Changes how the 1315 and 1323 condemnations should be narrated in John's biography: not as endpoints or defeats but as recurring occasions for a form of authorship he was already engaged in.
arguments.card: John's response to each condemnation was never simple retreat: the New Compilation, written in direct answer to the 1315 attack, leans more heavily on direct visionary authorization from the Virgin than its predecessor, and both compilations frame themselves through the Augustinian trope of "plundering the Egyptian treasure" — extracting what is genuinely sacred from a corrupted vehicle. Fanger's *Rewriting Magic* reads this pattern as continuous devotional labor, not merely defensive rewriting under institutional pressure (p.1–3).
arguments.body:
## The argument, precisely

Across two condemnations — 1315 and 1323 — John of Morigny's documented response was consistently to rewrite rather than to abandon his project of ritual composition. Fanger's monograph, titled *Rewriting Magic*, treats this pattern of revision itself as the central fact about John's authorship, arguing it should be read as continuous devotional and visionary labor rather than as a series of purely defensive retreats forced by institutional pressure.

## Against what

An alternative, more deflationary reading would treat each rewrite as simply damage control: a chastened author stripping out whatever specifically drew censure, producing a safer but diminished text each time. Fanger's framing resists this.

## Evidence

Internal textual strata show John was already revising the Old Compilation before any external condemnation forced his hand (*Rewriting Magic*, p.118) — revision was his working method independent of censure. The New Compilation, written urgently after 1315, does not retreat from visionary claims but leans on them more heavily. And both compilations frame the whole project through the "plundering the Egyptian treasure" trope (see [[plundering-egyptian-treasure]]), a constructive, not merely apologetic, self-understanding of what rewriting accomplishes (*Rewriting Magic*, p.2).

## Reception

This is this portal's own synthesis of the framing implicit in Fanger's monograph title and opening chapter, rather than a claim independently attributed to a named debate in the wider field; treated here as MEDIUM-confidence interpretive synthesis, not a directly quoted historiographical position.

## Literature

- Fanger, Claire. *Rewriting Magic*. Penn State University Press, 2015, p.1–3, p.118.

arguments.title: The historiography of erasure: how John lost his own book
arguments.claim: Across the centuries between 1323 and the 1990s rediscovery, successive paraphrases of the Grandes Chroniques' original notice did not merely compress John's story but progressively erased him as an author — culminating in Henry Charles Lea's 1887 history, which strips him of authorship of his own book entirely.
arguments.against: treating later secondary references to John as simply thinner or vaguer versions of the same basic, stable story
arguments.evidence: The chain runs: the 1323 Grandes Chroniques entry (roughly accurate, correctly distinguishes John's book from the ars notoria itself) -> Guillaume de Nangis's chronicle (compresses and blurs the account) -> a 16th-century Parisian antiquarian history that falsely credits the monk with inventing the ars notoria itself -> Lea's 1887 Inquisition history, which removes John as author altogether.
arguments.stakes: Demonstrates that what modern scholarship "knew" about John before the 1990s rediscovery was not a thin but accurate outline, but an actively degraded one — a caution about trusting any chain of paraphrase-of-paraphrase in the history of magic without checking the earliest link.
arguments.card: Between the 1323 burning and the 1990s rediscovery, successive retellings of John's story did not just get thinner — they got actively worse: from the *Grandes Chroniques*' roughly accurate 1323 notice, through Guillaume de Nangis's compression, to a 16th-century Parisian antiquarian history that falsely credits the unnamed monk with *inventing* the ars notoria, to Henry Charles Lea's 1887 history of the Inquisition, which strips him of authorship of his own book entirely. Fanger traces this chain as a caution about paraphrase-of-paraphrase historiography (*Rewriting Magic*, p.3, p.20–22).
arguments.body:
## The argument, precisely

Fanger traces a specific chain of textual transmission-by-paraphrase running from the 1323 *Grandes Chroniques de France* notice of John's condemnation through several intermediate retellings to Henry Charles Lea's 1887 *A History of the Inquisition of the Middle Ages*, arguing that each step did not merely compress the story but actively degraded its accuracy — culminating in an account that no longer credits John as the author of his own book at all.

## Against what

A naive reading of historiographical transmission might assume that later, thinner references to an obscure medieval figure are simply less detailed versions of an underlying stable fact-set. Fanger's traced chain shows the opposite: each retelling introduces new distortion, and the errors compound rather than average out.

## Evidence

The 1323 *Grandes Chroniques* notice, while judged by Fanger "inaccurate, if not unfair" on some points (e.g., its claim the book promised worldly riches), does at least correctly distinguish John's own book from the *ars notoria* tradition it draws on (*Rewriting Magic*, p.3). Guillaume de Nangis's chronicle entry compresses this further. A sixteenth-century antiquarian history of Paris (*Antiquitez... de Paris*, per the plan's own research notes) then falsely credits the unnamed monk with having *invented* the *ars notoria* itself — collapsing the crucial distinction the 1323 notice had preserved. Lea's 1887 Inquisition history, drawing on this degraded chain, removes John as an identifiable author altogether (*Rewriting Magic*, p.20–22).

## Reception

This chain is presented in Fanger's own preface/introduction as the historiographical backdrop against which the 1987–1990s manuscript rediscoveries (Dupèbe, Barnay, Kieckhefer, Watson, Fanger) should be understood — not as filling in a few missing details, but as recovering an author who had been genuinely lost from view through compounding misattribution.

## Literature

- Fanger, Claire. *Rewriting Magic*. Penn State University Press, 2015, p.3, p.20–22.

bibliography.author: Fanger, Claire
bibliography.title: Rewriting Magic: An Exegesis of the Visionary Autobiography of a Fourteenth-Century French Monk
bibliography.card: Fanger's own monograph-length study of John of Morigny, and the single work this portal draws on most heavily. Reads the *Liber florum* as visionary autobiography and traces its composition, condemnation, rewriting, and post-1323 survival, correcting several of Fanger's own earlier published claims (Bridget's name, the ars notoria's likely location at Orléans not Chartres, the "Barking Dogs'" location) in a candid 2015 preface.
bibliography.body:
## Bibliographic info

Claire Fanger, *Rewriting Magic: An Exegesis of the Visionary Autobiography of a Fourteenth-Century French Monk* (University Park: Penn State University Press, 2015).

## Argument and contribution

The book's central move is to read the *Liber florum celestis doctrine* as visionary autobiography — a genre claim that licenses treating John's own account of his visions, his relationship to the *ars notoria*, and his repeated rewriting under condemnation as a coherent, interpretable literary and devotional project rather than as incidental biographical noise around a magic text. Fanger traces the work's two-stage composition (Old and New Compilations), the specific 1315 and 1323 condemnations that shaped it, and argues that its post-1323 manuscript survival challenges standard assumptions about the effectiveness of medieval book censorship (see [[censorship-does-not-work]]).

## Key passages

- Preface (p.ix–xii): candid retraction of Fanger's own earlier claims — Bridget's name corrected from "Gurgeta/Georgette" to Burgeta; the ars notoria experiments relocated from Chartres to Orléans; the "Barking Dogs'" location at Sens retracted as a manuscript-reading error.
- p.1–3: opening frame — the *ars notoria*, the "plundering the Egyptian treasure" trope, the two condemnations.
- p.xiv–xvi: the *Liber florum*'s own structural table (Books of Visions/Prayers/Figures).
- p.20–22: the historiography-of-erasure chain and the censorship argument.
- p.105, p.118: 1315 condemnation detail; internal revision strata predating 1315.

## Reception

Not independently assessed for this portal beyond the book's own internal claims and its clear status as the current standard monograph on John of Morigny.

bibliography.body:
## Bibliographic info

Claire Fanger, ed., *Invoking Angels: Theurgic Ideas and Practices, Thirteenth to Sixteenth Centuries* (University Park: Penn State University Press, 2012).

## Argument and contribution

As an edited volume, its contribution to this portal is chapter-specific rather than a single thesis. Julien Véronèse's opening chapter, "Magic, Theurgy, and Spirituality in the Medieval Ritual of the *Ars notoria*" (translated by Fanger), lays out the ars notoria's textual structure, founding myth, and condemnation history in detail — this portal's [[ars-notoria]] and [[notae]] concept entries draw directly on it. Fanger's own chapter 5 undertakes a comparative reading of the *Liber iuratus Honorii* and the *Liber florum* around the shared theme of covenant and the divine name — not independently read in full for this Phase 1 build, flagged as a priority for a future pass.

## Key passages

- Véronèse, ch.1, p.37 (opening), p.41–44 (ars notoria structure, founding myth, condemnation).

## Argument and contribution

Provides the field's standard framework for distinguishing categories of medieval magic (natural magic, learned/ritual magic, necromancy) and situating clerical practitioners of ritual magic within an educated, often university-adjacent "clerical underworld." Used in this portal chiefly as context for John's own milieu at Orléans rather than as a source of John-specific claims.

bibliography.body:
## Bibliographic info

Claire Fanger and Nicholas Watson, "The Prologue to John of Morigny's *Liber Visionum*: Text and Translation," *Esoterica* 3 (2001).

## Argument and contribution

The first substantial English-language scholarly treatment of John of Morigny's text following the early-1990s manuscript rediscoveries, offering an edition and translation of the *Liber florum*'s prologue. Its lasting significance for this portal is historiographical rather than content-based: Fanger's own 2015 preface to *Rewriting Magic* explicitly retracts two claims first published here — the location of John's *ars notoria* experiments at Chartres (corrected to Orléans) and the location of the 1315 "Barking Dogs" condemnation at Sens (now treated as unlocated) — citing a manuscript-reading error in the original work (*Rewriting Magic*, p.x). This portal treats that retraction as a feature of the field's evidentiary discipline worth narrating explicitly, not a flaw to smooth over.
